title: Trust, but Verify: Tuning, Explaining & Uncertainty
subtitle: You told your boss the model scores 0.945. Tonight: the five questions a good boss asks next. Is that score real? Can we make it better? Why did it say that? How sure is it? Does it work for everyone? Cross-validation, honest tuning, SHAP, conformal prediction, slices and the model card

objectives.title: Report a Score You Can Stand Behind
objectives.description: One exam is partly luck: the same model scores anywhere from 0.938 to 0.947 depending on the shuffle. Five-fold cross-validation gives an average and a spread. And the exam must look like the real job: tested on next year's bookings, the same model scores about 0.88.

objectives.title: Tune Without Fooling Yourself
objectives.description: Dials are hyperparameters. Random search tries a dozen recipes and cross-validation does the tasting, with Optuna as the smarter optional version. The test set is opened once, at the end, because the best of many on the same exam is the luckiest.

objectives.title: Explain a Prediction With SHAP
objectives.description: Every prediction gets a receipt: start at the average booking, add each clue's push, arrive at the score. One booking explained in a sentence a manager can use, then the whole book. SHAP explains the model, not the world.

objectives.title: Say How Sure, and Check Who It Works For
objectives.description: Conformal prediction lets the model answer "will stay", "will cancel" or "not sure", with a promise it keeps. Slicing the mistakes by group shows who the model serves badly. The model card puts all of it on one honest page.

agenda.title: Five Questions From Your Boss
agenda.description: Last week's champion scores 0.945. You tell your boss. A good boss does not say "great": a good boss asks five questions. Tonight you learn to answer each one with evidence.
bulletPoints: A score is a claim: check it before you trust it
Tonight you play first: four small games in the Trust Explorer, one before each idea

agenda.title: Question 1: Is That Score Real?
agenda.description: Reshuffle the data eight times and the same model scores anywhere from 0.938 to 0.947. Five-fold cross-validation replaces one lucky exam with five and settles last week's question: boosting beats the forest on five exams out of five. Then the exam that looks like the real job: learn from 2015–16, predict 2017. The score drops to about 0.88.
bulletPoints: Report the average and the spread, not the luckiest exam
Choose the exam before the model: what will be new when the model is in use?

agenda.title: Question 2: Can We Make It Better?
agenda.description: Dials have a real name: hyperparameters. Random search bakes twelve recipes and cross-validation tastes them. Then the trap: the best of 200 models that know nothing scores 0.62 on a small exam and 0.50 on fresh bookings. Then the Tabular Frontier from Session 8: foundation models like TabPFN and TabICL that have read millions of tables and need no tuning at all.
bulletPoints: Choose with cross-validation; open the test set once
Tuning is the last few percent: 0.945 becomes 0.947
In 2026, a good analyst tries both: boosting and a tabular foundation model

agenda.title: Question 3: Why Did It Say That?
agenda.description: SHAP gives every prediction a receipt. Booking 438 scores 87%: it starts at the average of 37%, booking 312 days ahead adds 24 points, two changes to the booking take 10 away. Then all the receipts together: which clues drive the model, and in which direction.
bulletPoints: Local explanation: why this booking? Global explanation: what drives the model?
SHAP explains the model, not the world: the non-refundable deposit puzzle

agenda.title: Question 4: How Sure Is It?
agenda.description: Conformal prediction in four steps, by hand: a track-record pile, the model's surprise, the bar, and three possible answers. With a 90% promise the model commits on more than nine bookings in ten and says "not sure" on the rest.
bulletPoints: The "not sure" pile is the short list for a human
More certainty costs more "not sure": a business choice, not a math one

agenda.title: Question 5: Does It Work for Everyone? Your Turn
agenda.description: An average can hide a group. Missed cancels and false alarms by booking channel and by country, and what a manager does about the gaps. Everything from tonight goes on one page: the model card. Then four questions in the notebook.
bulletPoints: Guests booking from Portugal get more false alarms; direct bookings get most cancels missed
HW3 is due tonight; Milestone 2 Mon Nov 23, Milestone 3 Mon Nov 30

resources.title: Session 9 Slides — Trust, but Verify

Arrow keys to navigate, F for fullscreen, N for speaker notes.

resources.title: The Trust Explorer
resources.description: Four small games on tonight's hotel bookings, played before each idea. Reshuffle the exam and guess where the score lands. Make a model that knows nothing look like a real one. Call each clue up or down, then reveal the model's real receipt. And set the promise that decides which bookings go to a human. Works on your phone.

resources.title: Session 9 Notebook — Tuning, Explaining & Uncertainty
resources.description: Written for first-timers: five questions, eleven steps. Eight shuffles and five-fold cross-validation, the past-to-future exam, random search with an optional Optuna cell, the best-of-200-guessers trap, SHAP receipts for one booking and for the whole book, conformal prediction by hand, mistakes sliced by group, and a filled-in model card. Every step says what the cell does and how to read the output, with quick checks and four Your Turn questions.

resources.title: The SHAP Receipt
resources.description: SHAP from scratch, as a receipt. A trivia night shows the fair split: Ali, Bea and Cy seated in every order, then averaged. Then Maya's loan: drag her income or missed payments and the receipt reprints, shuffle the order the clues arrive in, watch the fairness rules check themselves, and stack 120 receipts to see how the model thinks. Ends with the fine print and three quick questions. Works on your phone.

resources.title: The SHAP Receipt — Notebook
resources.description: Written for first-timers. Split the trivia prize by hand, build a loan model, then compute Maya's SHAP receipt yourself with a loop and an average, and check that the shap library gets the same numbers. Then the waterfall, beeswarm, bar and scatter plots, sliders, what happens when you change the comparison crowd, and three Your Turn challenges. Runtime → Run all.

resources.title: The Tabular Frontier — Slides
resources.description: Opening Day: a new hotel with only 200 bookings. Why small data hurts (our model drops from 0.945 to 0.80), the fresh graduate and the experienced manager, a model that read millions of made-up tables, your rows as the prompt, the race, and which one to use when. Arrow keys to navigate, N for speaker notes.

resources.title: The Tabular Frontier — Notebook
resources.description: Written for first-timers. A learning curve from 50 to 24,000 bookings, made-up tables you can solve yourself, in-context learning in plain words, and a race between gradient boosting and TabICL (an open-source tabular foundation model) on a new hotel with 100, 300 and 1,000 bookings. Use a T4 GPU runtime.

resources.title: The Conformal Explorer
resources.description: Set a coverage target, watch the calibration residuals size the band, then draw new cases a hundred times and check the promise. Underfit the model, shrink the calibration set, or shift the data to see what breaks it.

resources.title: MLU-Explain — Cross-Validation
resources.description: K-fold, animated: watch the folds rotate and the estimate stabilize.

resources.title: Angelopoulos & Bates — A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction
resources.description: The self-contained tutorial that made conformal prediction mainstream: the split-conformal recipe, coverage guarantees, and extensions to classification, time series, and distribution shift.

resources.title: Google PAIR — Measuring Fairness
resources.description: An explorable on why equal accuracy can hide unequal error rates, and the trade-offs between fairness definitions. Do this before the fairness-slicing lab.

resources.title: MLU-Explain — Equality of Odds
resources.description: A fairness criterion you can drag: equalize true- and false-positive rates across groups and see what it costs.

resources.title: Molnar — Interpretable Machine Learning (free book)
resources.description: The reference for SHAP, partial dependence, ICE, permutation importance, and counterfactuals — with the honest caveats for each.

resources.title: Fairlearn
resources.description: Microsoft's open-source toolkit for assessing and mitigating fairness issues: MetricFrame for sliced metrics is the one-liner behind tonight's fairness section.

resources.title: scikit-learn User Guide — Cross-Validation: Evaluating Estimator Performance
resources.description: Every splitter with a picture: KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit. The visualization section alone is worth the visit.

resources.title: SHAP Documentation — An Introduction to Explainable AI With Shapley Values
resources.description: The canonical walkthrough from the library's authors: what Shapley values are, why they are the fair attribution, and how to read every plot type we use tonight.

resources.title: MAPIE — Model-Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator
resources.description: scikit-learn-contrib's conformal prediction library. Tonight we build conformal prediction by hand in ten lines; MAPIE is what you use at work (SplitConformalClassifier for yes/no, SplitConformalRegressor for numbers). The theory pages are short and readable.

resources.title: Optuna — Hyperparameter Optimization Framework
resources.description: Define an objective, call study.optimize, read study.best_params. The optional cell in tonight's notebook is the tutorial's first example, applied to the hotel model.

resources.title: Kaggle Learn — Machine Learning Explainability
resources.description: Permutation importance, partial dependence, and SHAP values in four short lessons with exercises. The fastest path to fluency before Milestone 3.

resources.title: Story: A Readmission Model Rebuilt for Equity at ZSFG
resources.description: Zuckerberg San Francisco General replaced a vendor readmission model with an in-house gradient-boosted tree that includes social-determinants data — and reports lower readmissions and narrower equity gaps. Explanation, slicing, and monitoring in a real hospital.

resources.title: Mitchell et al. (2019) — Model Cards for Model Reporting
resources.description: The paper that defined the one-page model card: intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, ethical considerations, caveats. Your final project includes one.

resources.title: Refresher: Müller & Guido, Ch. 5 — Cross-Validation & Grid Search (official notebook)
resources.description: k-fold, stratified, leave-one-out, shuffle-split, and grouped cross-validation, then grid search with nested CV. The slow version of tonight's first hour.

activities.title: Explain It, Bound It, Slice It
activities.description: Take tonight's tuned hotel model. Check its score with ten exams instead of five, explain a booking of your choice with a SHAP receipt, change the conformal promise, and slice the mistakes by a column you are curious about. Each question has a starter cell in the notebook.

steps.title: More exams
steps.description: Run cross-validation with 10 parts instead of 5. Does the average change? Does the spread?

steps.title: Explain
steps.description: Print the receipt for booking 2, 7 or 103 and write the sentence you would say to the front-desk manager.

steps.title: Change the promise
steps.description: Try a promise of 0.97, then 0.80. What happens to the "not sure" pile, and what new answer appears at 0.80?

steps.title: Slice
steps.description: Missed cancels and false alarms by customer_type, deposit_type or arrival_date_year. Which group does the model serve worst?

activities.discussionNote: Five questions a boss will ask, five tools. Is the score real? Cross-validation, on an exam that looks like the job. Can it be better? Tuning, judged by cross-validation. Why did it say that? The SHAP receipt. How sure is it? The conformal answer; the bookings labeled "not sure" are exactly the ones a human should look at. Does it work for everyone? The sliced mistakes. The model card is where the answers live.

takeaways.text: A score is a claim. Check it. One exam is partly luck: use cross-validation and report the average and the spread. And make the exam look like the real job: 0.945 shuffled is about 0.88 on next year's bookings.
Choose with cross-validation, open the test set once. SHAP then gives every prediction a receipt. It explains the model's score; it does not tell you what happens if you change a policy.
Let the model say "not sure", and check who it works for. Conformal prediction keeps an honest promise, slices show the groups an average hides, and the model card puts it all on one page.
